lead: The link power budget adds every loss between transmitter and receiver, plus a reserve, and compares the total with the power the transmitter gives and the receiver needs. The reserve keeps the link working after connectors wear, repair splices are added and the laser ages. Designers use the budget to choose the source, fiber, joints and receiver; if the losses fit, the link closes.
prereq: You need fiber attenuation in dB/km, splice and connector losses, and receiver sensitivity.

blocks.text: P<sub>T</sub> is the mean power launched into the fiber, in dBm. P<sub>R</sub> is the receiver sensitivity: the smallest mean power, in dBm, that gives the required BER at the bit rate. P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> is the loss you can afford, in dB.
P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> = αL + l<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + l<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + M
blocks.where: P<sub>T</sub> is launched power in dBm; P<sub>R</sub> is receiver sensitivity in dBm; α is fiber attenuation in dB/km; L is fiber length in km; l<sub>c</sub> is the loss per connector in dB and N<sub>c</sub> the number of connectors; l<sub>s</sub> is the loss per splice in dB and N<sub>s</sub> the number of splices; M is the system margin in dB.

blocks.text: Both sides are in dB. M is not a loss you can measure on a new link but a reserve for source ageing, temperature, repair splices and extra patch cords: usually 6 dB, 3 to 4 dB for a short indoor link.

The received power is P<sub>T</sub> minus the physical losses only, in dBm. The spare margin is what is left after the reserve: spare = (P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub>) − (αL + l<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + l<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + M). A spare of zero or more closes the budget.

The receiver has a ceiling too: overload, the largest power before the preamplifier saturates. The received power must lie between P<sub>R</sub> and overload; a short link with a strong laser needs a fixed attenuator.
Use planning values, not the best laboratory number:

Count joints carefully: connectors at both ends and at every patch panel; one splice between reels, so 60 km in 10 km reels has five splices. A link near its dispersion limit needs a little more power because spread pulses close the eye; this dispersion power penalty, typically 1 to 2 dB, is one more loss term.
Write the budget as a table, losses in the order the light meets them; here for the worked example's 60 km link:

If the spare is negative, cutting M to make it fit only hides risk. Change a real term: a shorter span, lower-loss fiber, fewer joints, a stronger source, an APD instead of a pin, or an amplifier. A large spare may mean you paid for a laser the link did not need.
Whether the pulses are still sharp at that distance is the job of the rise-time budget; the link must pass both.

spec.aria: Graph of power in dBm against distance from 0 to 60 kilometres. The line falls from 0 dBm to minus 14.7 dBm with small steps at five splices. Dashed lines mark the sensitivity at minus 28 dBm and overload at minus 8 dBm. A stacked bar at the end shows 6 dB margin and 7.3 dB spare.

examples.question: Design check for a 2.5 Gbit/s link: a 1550 nm laser launches 0 dBm into 60 km of single-mode fiber with α = 0.22 dB/km, laid in 10 km reels joined by fusion splices of 0.1 dB each. There is one connector of 0.5 dB at each end. The receiver sensitivity is −28 dBm at 2.5 Gbit/s and its overload level is −8 dBm. A 6 dB system margin is required. Does the budget close? Find the received power and the spare margin.
steps: Splices: 60 km in 10 km reels is 6 reels, so N<sub>s</sub> = 6 − 1 = 5 splices inside the span. The two ends are connectors, N<sub>c</sub> = 2.
Losses: fiber 0.22 × 60 = 13.2 dB, connectors 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 dB, splices 5 × 0.1 = 0.5 dB; physical total 14.7 dB, so the received power is −14.7 dBm.
Overload: −14.7 dBm is below −8 dBm, so no attenuator is needed. Available 0 − (−28) = 28 dB; used with margin 14.7 + 6 = 20.7 dB.
Spare = 28 − 20.7 = 7.3 dB. Check: −14.7 dBm is 13.3 dB above sensitivity, 6 dB reserve plus 7.3 dB spare.
examples.answer: It closes: 20.7 dB used of 28 dB, a spare of 7.3 dB, and −14.7 dBm received, between sensitivity and overload.

examples.question: A building link uses an 850 nm LED that couples −13 dBm into 62.5 µm multimode fiber, a silicon pin receiver with a sensitivity of −38 dBm at 20 Mbit/s, two connectors of 1.0 dB each, and cable with 3.0 dB/km including its splices. With a 6 dB margin, what is the longest link the power budget allows?
steps: Fixed losses and reserve: connectors 2 × 1.0 = 2 dB, margin 6 dB, total 8 dB.
Check: 3.0 × 5.67 + 2 + 6 = 25 dB, exactly the available power.
examples.answer: About 5.7 km. Beyond that the LED link needs a laser, a lower-loss window or an APD.

traps: Adding a dBm value to a dB value. P<sub>T</sub>, P<sub>R</sub> and the received power are in dBm; the losses and the margin are in dB.
Leaving the margin out of the used total, or putting it into the received power. The received power counts physical losses only; the margin is held back from the spare.
Miscounting joints: 60 km in 10 km reels has five splices, not six, and both end connectors count.
Treating sensitivity as the only limit. A short link with a strong laser can exceed the overload level and fail from too much light.
Leaving out the dispersion power penalty when the link is close to its dispersion limit.

quiz.q: Write the link power-budget equation and give the unit of each symbol.
quiz.a: P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> = αL + l<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + l<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + M. P<sub>T</sub> and P<sub>R</sub> in dBm; α in dB/km; L in km; l<sub>c</sub>, l<sub>s</sub> and M in dB; N<sub>c</sub> and N<sub>s</sub> are counts.

quiz.q: Why is the system margin added as a loss when it cannot be measured on the new link?
quiz.a: It reserves power for losses that will appear later: source ageing, temperature, repair splices and extra patch cords. Adding it checks that the received power still stays above sensitivity after those changes.

quiz.q: A 1550 nm link has P<sub>T</sub> = 1 dBm, P<sub>R</sub> = −30 dBm, L = 80 km, α = 0.22 dB/km, two connectors of 0.5 dB, seven splices of 0.1 dB and M = 5 dB. Find the spare margin.
quiz.a: Fiber 80 × 0.22 = 17.6 dB, connectors 1.0 dB, splices 0.7 dB, margin 5 dB: used 24.3 dB. Available 1 − (−30) = 31 dB. Spare = 31 − 24.3 = 6.7 dB, so it closes.

quiz.q: An LED launches −13 dBm into 500 m of multimode fiber at 3.0 dB/km with two connectors of 1 dB each and no splices. P<sub>R</sub> = −30 dBm and M = 4 dB. Find the received power and the spare margin.
quiz.a: Physical loss 1.5 + 2.0 = 3.5 dB, so the received power is −16.5 dBm. Used with margin 7.5 dB; available 17 dB; spare 9.5 dB.

quiz.q: Distinguish receiver sensitivity from receiver overload.
quiz.a: Sensitivity is the smallest mean power that gives the required BER; overload is the largest power before the receiver saturates and the BER rises again. The received power must lie between them.

quiz.q: A design shows a spare margin of −2 dB. Give two changes that close it, with the dB each gains.
quiz.a: Shorten the span by 10 km at 0.22 dB/km: gains 2.2 dB. Or use a source 3 dB stronger (0 dBm to 3 dBm): gains 3 dB. An APD receiver, typically 5 to 10 dB more sensitive, also works. Cutting the margin is not a valid fix.

beyond: Amplified long-haul systems are budgeted by optical signal-to-noise ratio as well as power, and forward error correction lowers the power a receiver needs. Search for OSNR budget and FEC coding gain.
